claims.text: Eutectic alloy design producing a fine alternating soft/hard lamellar microstructure can concurrently improve strength and ductility.
Conventional cast AlCoCrFeNi-based high-entropy alloys may have coarse or segregated microstructures, poor ductility, and inferior castability.
Vacuum induction melting can be used to prepare an AlCoCrFeNi-based eutectic high-entropy alloy.
Eutectic processing can produce a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure in an AlCoCrFeNi-based alloy.
Controlled cooling promotes eutectic solidification and formation of the desired lamellar structure.
Limited cold rolling further refines the lamellar microstructure.
The as-cast eutectic alloy can exhibit a fine fcc/B2 lamellar microstructure with an interlamellar spacing of about 2 micrometres.
The fcc phase is soft and ductile and provides excellent dislocation storage.
The B2 or bcc phase is hard, pins dislocations, and provides high strength.
Alternating soft and hard phases promote high strain hardening through dislocation accumulation in the ductile phase and restriction of dislocation motion at phase boundaries.
The enhanced strain hardening delays necking and fracture.
An AlCoCrFeNi-based eutectic alloy can achieve tensile or fracture strength near 1 GPa.
An AlCoCrFeNi-based eutectic alloy can achieve elongation exceeding 20–25% at room temperature.
The eutectic-processed alloy has significantly greater strength and elongation than a conventional cast alloy.
High-entropy alloys lacking an engineered fine lamellar structure generally exhibit either high strength with low ductility or high ductility with inadequate strength.
The eutectic design approach is effective at room temperature.
The approach remains effective at moderately elevated temperatures relevant to structural applications.
Poor control of phase spacing or scale-up-induced segregation can limit the benefits of eutectic alloy design.
